ELECTION 2016

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
26,3 million SAns were registered to vote. But how many cast their votes and what will the results be and mean for the future of South Africa?

Further information:
The fifth local government election since our country’s democracy has been billed the country’s most important election since 1994. The African National Congress, which has governed since then, is widely expected to lose its dominance in some strategic municipalities. But whether it loses, or hangs on by the skin of its teeth, the ANC will confront a crucial choice: own up to the problems that have caused its decline and correct them. Or march on, relying on the leadership that has failed it. A record 63 654 candidates competed for the support of a record 26,3 million registered voters.
Before voting day on Wednesday, one in 10 voters remained undecided about who they will vote for.
The local government election is the barometre of the depth of democracy. Some commentators have said that this election could either reassure South Africans that our democracy is still in fairly good health and our stability strong enough for now, or or it could quickly drag us further down the spiral of regression. Opposition parties have called time on the ANC’s dominance.
The political temperature has not been this high since 1994. Twenty election candidates have been murdered and hundreds of millions of rands lost through damage to property during political protests.
Politicians – and President Jacob Zuma – used pre-election rhetoric of a kind not seen before. The main reason probably was because the past week’s election was the prelude to the mother of all elections in 2019 – and more was at stake than merely the number of wards or councils lost or won.
During one of the last ANC rallies, President Jacob Zuma told thousands of supporters in Zulu: “The oppressors still control the economy. The black nation must unite until the land is returned.” The appeal was blatant and painted the DA – the biggest opposition party – as a “white” organisation that must be fought by South Africa’s black majority. At campaign rally after campaign rally, the President has recalled the battles of the apartheid era, denounding the DA as a “poisonous snake” filled with “hatred” of black people.
High and rising unemployment, corruption and poor service delivery have been some of the main issues dominating the election campaign. At least 26% of South Africans are without work. The ANC has been hit by a string of scandals this year – the Concourt ruling that President Zuma should personally be held liable to pay back millions of his Nkandla home, the High Court ruling that charges should be reinstated against him in regard with the Spy Tapes saga and the alleged involvement of the Gupta family in what was coined “State Capture”. According to Municipal IQ, a data and intelligence service specilaising in the monitoring and assessment of South Africa’s 287 municipalities, there were at least 70 violent protests over a lack of decent housing, other service delivery issues and education since the beginning of the year. In 2015, there were 44 protests within the same period.
The unresponsiveness of government is a driver of community protest, but it is not the only driver of dissent. Commentators say one cannot separate local government from thje socio-economic conditions in which it operates.
The ANC knew that if current trends continued and it got less that 60% of the electoral support, there would be a realistic chance that it could get less than 50% of the vote in 2019. And there is the chance that if the EFF didn’t at least doubled its support of 6% in the 2014 general election, South Africans would not take it as seriously as they did until now.
But what will the results reflect? And with a voting day that more or less ran smoothly and without the violence that was expected, do South Africans feel more positive about the years ahead and what the general election of 2019 will bring us?
How many of the 26,3 million registered voters drew their crosses? At the 2011 local government election, 23 million people were registered, but only 11 million voted.
South Africans will probably feel even more positive if the coalitions between political parties to govern cities and towns actually work and last. But can political parties like the ANC and the DA or the ANC and the EFF govern together and will they even consider coalition to create a better future for the citizens of our country? And if the ANC doesn’t get an outright majority in 2019, the whole country will have to be governed by a coalition. That could mean a serious test for stability and effective government.
How do political parties that govern municipalities and councils obtain stability and progress? What is necessary to get that universal political reality of a strong centre and a solid middle ground?
What will this election’s results show? There were three highly contested Metro’s – Johannesburg, Tswane and Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality in Port Elizabeth. Rustenburg in Northwest might for the first time fall into the governing hands of the EFF.
In 2011, the ANC managed to secure control of 198 councils, winning in seven of the country’s eight biggest Metropolitian areas. Some 40% of the country live in those areas. In contrast, the DA, with Cape Town under its control, managed 18 councils. Beaufort-West was the only municipality in the Western Cape that was still managed by the ANC.
How much support will 35-year old leftist firebrand, Julius Malema, leader of the EFF, get? And will the EFF form coalitions with the DA in order to oust the ANC in some municipalities?
South Africa is one of the most powerful engines in the African economy, yet many will argue that the ANC’s policies have led to the economic stagnation and rising unemployment. If the leading party’s results are worse than expected, and internal revolt could force President Zuma to quit, leading to economic reforms that could boost growth in South Africa and the rest of the continent. But a strong ANC majority would keep him in power and allow him to influence the succession until he steps down in 2019.
The country is hurting economically. Since the currency plunged to record lows in December after President Zuma fired former Finance Minister Nhlanha Nene, the International Monetary Fund has slashed its forecast for South Africa, projecting growth of only 0,1 percent this year. And the central bank is now forecasting zero growth this year.

Press Release:


Voice of the People
South Africans this week voted in arguably the most contested local government election yet. With political parties grappling for control over South Africa’s eight key metros, there’s little doubt of the significance of the 2016 Municipal vote. Carte Blanche brings key analysis to a ballot that’s seen both the ruling party and opposition face their greatest tests since the onset of democratic rule.


Script:


ELECTION 2016

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: BONGANI BINGWA

BROADCAST DATE: 7 AUGUST 2016

JULIUS MALEMA: The ANC is arrogant and I have given myself a personal task to ensure that in my lifetime, I want to see the ANC out of power.

ZWELINZIMA VAVI: Once an Organistaion that enjoyed two thirds, is suddenly below 50%, it only means that the people have spoken.

MMUSI MAIMANE: We have shown ourselves to be the only alternative. We have shown ourselves to be that alternative that can show South Africans the way forward.

ZIZI KODWA: The results indicate that we still have a confidence in an ANC elect, in the ANC led by President Zuma.

BONGANI OPENING LINK: These have arguably been South Africa’s most hotly contested local government elections yet with South Africa’s 8 metros up for grabs. It’s a poll that has seen both the governing party and the opposition face their stiffest challenges up to date.

In what may prove to be a watershed election, the clear dominance of the ANC since the dawn of democracy has been shaken, says political commentator, Professor Tinyiko Maluleke.

PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: The Anc has always assumed 50 plus 1 and now they can’t.

The key battles were fought in four of the country’s eight Metropolitian Municipalities, namely the City of Cape Town, Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality in Port Elizabeth, the City of Johannesburg and the City of Tswane.

The Democratic Alliance has made significant inroads in all of these, but the emergence of the EFF – has dramatically changed the political landscape.

PROF. TINYIKO MALULEKE: They have brought their own sense of urgency, they have upped the tempo of political discourse.

EFF National Chairperson, advocate Dali Mpofu, says they are satisfied with the election results, after securing almost 8% of the total votes. They’ve also won eight wards, but no municipalities.

ADV DALI MPOFU: IT COULDN’T GET better than this. You know, when you are bringing to size the ANC which is a serious brand even in business terms. We been sitting in our wars rooms for months planning for this moment.

In 2011, the ANC won 198 councils and took control of 7 of the country’s metros.
Although this election should have been primarily about local governance issues, Prof Maluleke says the spectre of President Jacob Zuma would have loomed large in many voters’ minds.

PROF. TINYIKO MALULEKE: Jacob Zuma as a national issue has dominated this elections.

Throughout his campaign, DA leader Mmusi Maimane said the elections would be a referendum about President Jacob Zuma.

MMUSI MAIMANE: A - you can’t violate the constitution and B - you can’t continue theme of corruption and get away with it.

Former trade unionist Zwelinzima Vavi agrees that many ANC-supporters have lost confidence in the governing party’s leadership.

VAVI: If he was a leader of any party that cares about its future, he would do the right thing. But he won’t.

But the ANC’s Zizi Kodwa says the ANC’s overall results are a reflection of the party’s successful campaign.

ZIZI KODWA: If you look at the national percentage, the next party will always be 20-something… Not even half of what the ANC enjoys.

BONGANI LINK: Overall the ANC remains the dominant party, but most South Africans live in the cities and not in the rural areas. So, if opposition parties continue to make inroads into that urban voter base, we are stepping into unchartered territory.

ZWELINZIMA VAVI: I warned aganst this happening ten, 15 years ago. I said unless the ANC can stop their own goals that it was scoring left and right and centre, what will happen eventually is that the working class will start losing hope. They will not vote for another party.

Which is what happened in the troubled Vuwani area in Limpopo where only 1600 out of 44-thousand registered voters cast their votes. The defence force was sent to guard against violence in Vuwani after some residents threatened to keep the community away from polling stations. During violent protests earlier this year, 27 schools were burnt down over municipal demarcation.

DALI MPOFU: They start by losing the urban base and there will be a time where the ANC will be simply be a rural party. And that is why our campaign, if you have noticed, is tackling both the urban and the rural base.

In the Eastern Cape Metro of Buffalo City, Mangaung in the Free State, Ethekwini in Kwazulu Natal and Ekurhuleni on the East Rand the ANC retained its power.

Fifty-eight percent of SA’S 26,3 million registered voters cast their ballots in what has proved to be the most unpredictable election since 1994.

But why did only 14 million people vote when 12-million more were registered?

PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: I also think the South African voter has become slightly more sophisticated over the years, slightly more demanding.

Since the beginning of 2016, there have been more than a hundred violent protests over the lack of basic service delivery and housing, and this has probably contributed to voter apathy.

PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: Those issues account in some ways both for growth that the DA has seen and the growth that the EFF has seen.

BONGANI: We used to talk about the ANC in terms of how significant its majories would be and now the discussion is whether or not they will even have one.

ZWELINZIMA VAVI: What a sad moment. I mean, in such a short period of time - it has taken Comrade Jacob Zuma about seven years – seven years to destroy a Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Chris Hani, Chief Luthuli’s movement.

BONGANI LINK CAPE TOWN: It was ten years ago that the DA wrested control of the Cape metropole from the ANC in a coalition with smaller parties. Since then it has entrenched its base and Cape Town delivered the largest majority for any party in 2016

The DA was victorius with an overwhelming 66% against the 24% which the ANC was able to rake in. The DA also managed to get the majority vote in previously ANC held municipalities in the Western Cape, such as Beaufort West.

ZWELINZIMA VAVI: The ANC lost cape town not because the DA was better but because the ANC was so bad.

Zizi Kodwa admits that the party has made some mistakes and should correct them.

ZIZI KODWA: A vote against the ANC sometimes is not an anti-ANC vote. It is an expression of unhappiness. Maybe it says something to the ANC. But the strength of the ANC is we acknowledge, we own up our mistakes, but also we self-correct.

BONGANI LINK: At its peak, the ANC’s majority in Nelson Mandela Bay was 66,5% in 2006 when Thabo Mbeki was President. Under Jacob Zuma, it fell by 15% in 2011. Then came the disaster of 2016 – it’s down to 40,8%. That means in ten years, the party has lost an astounding 25% of its support in this metro.

The DA has increased its support by 22% over the last ten years, securing a comfortable victory with a total of 46% of the votes.

MMUSI MAIMANE: If you ask people in Nelson Mandela Bay what they voted for, when you ask them again, they say: “We voted for ‘Change’.” I think, that to me, says our message got through.

BONGANI LINK: In Gauteng, the ANC’s decline first became apparent with the public booing of President Zuma at Nelson Mandela’s memorial in 2013. With a large concentration of urban voters in Johannesburg and Tshwane, there was bound to be a backlash at a number of issues.

The battle for the Cities of Tswane and Johannesburg has been neck-and-neck until the very end.
In Tshwane the DA celebrated victory over the ANC with 43% against 41%.

This means that coalitions between political parties will be formed to create a majority. But when yesterday’s enemies become tomorrow’s friends, it could lead to a rocky relationship.

The EFF has been punted as the kingmakers, with the potential of entering into coalitions in the hanging metros.

JULIUS MALEMA: We are not prepared to speak to the ANC or engage in any form of coalition with the ANC.

BONGANI: Many will say these coalitions are marriages of convenience as they are doomed to fail?

DALI MPOFU: We are not saying we will work with DA or the UDM or the Freedom Front. We are saying all opposition parties, if the opposition is in a position to form a government we need to get together as opposition parties and say the people have rejected the ANC, what do we do now?

But the ANC will not take any of this lying down.

BONGANI: So how much can we take out of all of this as a prelude to 2019 when President Zuma won’t be running anymore?

PROF. TINYIKO MALULEKE: I think 2019 will be tighter than we have seen at local elections.

DALI MPOFU: The ANC will be contending against in 2019 will be weakened, because whatever happens there is going to be a bruising leadership battle for next year for 2017.

MMUSI MAIMANE: Looking at this year’s results, of course we got to use those as a benchmark to say what we do in 2019.

ZIZI: We must not take the outcome of this election for granted in terms of the expectation of people. The more we realize that these people have voted us almost ten million of them, they have expectation in ANC

A new era has dawned in South African politics – voters demand real performance from the party in power.

PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: These elections have proved that Nkandla does actually matter even to the poor. Not Nkandla in itself, but what it symbolises, what it stands for and what it stands for is a failure of leadership and a failure of governance and I think people are beginning to get that message.


PROMO’S
PROMO 1: 15”
PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: The ANC has always assumed 50 plus 1 and now they can’t.

JULIUS MALEMA: We will not enter any coalition with the ANC.
In what may prove to be a watershed election, the ANC’s dominance has been shaken.
PROMO 2: 15”
JULIUS MALEMA: In my lifetime, I want to see the ANC out of power.

ZIZI KODWA: The results indicate that we still have a confidence in an ANC led by President Zuma.

The most hotly contested elections since the dawn of democracy. But how will it take the country forward?

EFF National Chairperson, advocate Dali Mpofu, says they are satisfied with the election results, after securing almost 8% of the total votes. They’ve also won eight wards, but no municipalities. ADV DALI MPOFU: IT COULDN’T GET better than this. You know, when you are bringing to size the ANC which is a serious brand even in business terms. We been sitting in our wars rooms for months planning for this moment. In 2011, the ANC won 198 councils and took control of 7 of the country’s metros. Although this election should have been primarily about local governance issues, Prof Maluleke says the spectre of President Jacob Zuma would have loomed large in many voters’ minds. PROF. TINYIKO MALULEKE: Jacob Zuma as a national issue has dominated this elections. Throughout his campaign, DA leader Mmusi Maimane said the elections would be a referendum about President Jacob Zuma. MMUSI MAIMANE: A - you can’t violate the constitution and B - you can’t continue theme of corruption and get away with it. Former trade unionist Zwelinzima Vavi agrees that many ANC-supporters have lost confidence in the governing party’s leadership. VAVI: If he was a leader of any party that cares about its future, he would do the right thing. But he won’t. But the ANC’s Zizi Kodwa says the ANC’s overall results are a reflection of the party’s successful campaign. ZIZI KODWA: If you look at the national percentage, the next party will always be 20-something… Not even half of what the ANC enjoys. BONGANI LINK: Overall the ANC remains the dominant party, but most South Africans live in the cities and not in the rural areas. So, if opposition parties continue to make inroads into that urban voter base, we are stepping into unchartered territory. ZWELINZIMA VAVI: I warned aganst this happening ten, 15 years ago. I said unless the ANC can stop their own goals that it was scoring left and right and centre, what will happen eventually is that the working class will start losing hope. They will not vote for another party. Which is what happened in the troubled Vuwani area in Limpopo where only 1600 out of 44-thousand registered voters cast their votes. The defence force was sent to guard against violence in Vuwani after some residents threatened to keep the community away from polling stations. During violent protests earlier this year, 27 schools were burnt down over municipal demarcation. DALI MPOFU: They start by losing the urban base and there will be a time where the ANC will be simply be a rural party. And that is why our campaign, if you have noticed, is tackling both the urban and the rural base. In the Eastern Cape Metro of Buffalo City, Mangaung in the Free State, Ethekwini in Kwazulu Natal and Ekurhuleni on the East Rand the ANC retained its power. Fifty-eight percent of SA’S 26,3 million registered voters cast their ballots in what has proved to be the most unpredictable election since 1994. But why did only 14 million people vote when 12-million more were registered? PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: I also think the South African voter has become slightly more sophisticated over the years, slightly more demanding. Since the beginning of 2016, there have been more than a hundred violent protests over the lack of basic service delivery and housing, and this has probably contributed to voter apathy. PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: Those issues account in some ways both for growth that the DA has seen and the growth that the EFF has seen. BONGANI: We used to talk about the ANC in terms of how significant its majories would be and now the discussion is whether or not they will even have one. ZWELINZIMA VAVI: What a sad moment. I mean, in such a short period of time - it has taken Comrade Jacob Zuma about seven years – seven years to destroy a Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Chris Hani, Chief Luthuli’s movement. BONGANI LINK CAPE TOWN: It was ten years ago that the DA wrested control of the Cape metropole from the ANC in a coalition with smaller parties. Since then it has entrenched its base and Cape Town delivered the largest majority for any party in 2016 The DA was victorius with an overwhelming 66% against the 24% which the ANC was able to rake in. The DA also managed to get the majority vote in previously ANC held municipalities in the Western Cape, such as Beaufort West. ZWELINZIMA VAVI: The ANC lost cape town not because the DA was better but because the ANC was so bad. Zizi Kodwa admits that the party has made some mistakes and should correct them. ZIZI KODWA: A vote against the ANC sometimes is not an anti-ANC vote. It is an expression of unhappiness. Maybe it says something to the ANC. But the strength of the ANC is we acknowledge, we own up our mistakes, but also we self-correct. BONGANI LINK: At its peak, the ANC’s majority in Nelson Mandela Bay was 66,5% in 2006 when Thabo Mbeki was President. Under Jacob Zuma, it fell by 15% in 2011. Then came the disaster of 2016 – it’s down to 40,8%. That means in ten years, the party has lost an astounding 25% of its support in this metro. The DA has increased its support by 22% over the last ten years, securing a comfortable victory with a total of 46% of the votes. MMUSI MAIMANE: If you ask people in Nelson Mandela Bay what they voted for, when you ask them again, they say: “We voted for ‘Change’.” I think, that to me, says our message got through. BONGANI LINK: In Gauteng, the ANC’s decline first became apparent with the public booing of President Zuma at Nelson Mandela’s memorial in 2013. With a large concentration of urban voters in Johannesburg and Tshwane, there was bound to be a backlash at a number of issues. The battle for the Cities of Tswane and Johannesburg has been neck-and-neck until the very end. In Tshwane the DA celebrated victory over the ANC with 43% against 41%. This means that coalitions between political parties will be formed to create a majority. But when yesterday’s enemies become tomorrow’s friends, it could lead to a rocky relationship. The EFF has been punted as the kingmakers, with the potential of entering into coalitions in the hanging metros. JULIUS MALEMA: We are not prepared to speak to the ANC or engage in any form of coalition with the ANC. BONGANI: Many will say these coalitions are marriages of convenience as they are doomed to fail? DALI MPOFU: We are not saying we will work with DA or the UDM or the Freedom Front. We are saying all opposition parties, if the opposition is in a position to form a government we need to get together as opposition parties and say the people have rejected the ANC, what do we do now? But the ANC will not take any of this lying down. BONGANI: So how much can we take out of all of this as a prelude to 2019 when President Zuma won’t be running anymore? PROF. TINYIKO MALULEKE: I think 2019 will be tighter than we have seen at local elections. DALI MPOFU: The ANC will be contending against in 2019 will be weakened, because whatever happens there is going to be a bruising leadership battle for next year for 2017. MMUSI MAIMANE: Looking at this year’s results, of course we got to use those as a benchmark to say what we do in 2019. ZIZI: We must not take the outcome of this election for granted in terms of the expectation of people. The more we realize that these people have voted us almost ten million of them, they have expectation in ANC A new era has dawned in South African politics – voters demand real performance from the party in power. PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: These elections have proved that Nkandla does actually matter even to the poor. Not Nkandla in itself, but what it symbolises, what it stands for and what it stands for is a failure of leadership and a failure of governance and I think people are beginning to get that message. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” PROF TINYIKO MALULEKE: The ANC has always assumed 50 plus 1 and now they can’t. JULIUS MALEMA: We will not enter any coalition with the ANC. In what may prove to be a watershed election, the ANC’s dominance has been shaken. PROMO 2: 15” JULIUS MALEMA: In my lifetime, I want to see the ANC out of power. ZIZI KODWA: The results indicate that we still have a confidence in an ANC led by President Zuma. The most hotly contested elections since the dawn of democracy. But how will it take the country forward? Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for ELECTION 2016 (4839) Este de Klerk 10 August 2016

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): 26,3 million SAns were registered to vote. But how many cast their votes and what will the results be and mean for the future of South Africa?
metadata.Further information: The fifth local government election since our country’s democracy has been billed the country’s most important election since 1994. The African National Congress, which has governed since then, is widely expected to lose its dominance in some strategic municipalities. But whether it loses, or hangs on by the skin of its teeth, the ANC will confront a crucial choice: own up to the problems that have caused its decline and correct them. Or march on, relying on the leadership that has failed it. A record 63 654 candidates competed for the support of a record 26,3 million registered voters. Before voting day on Wednesday, one in 10 voters remained undecided about who they will vote for. The local government election is the barometre of the depth of democracy. Some commentators have said that this election could either reassure South Africans that our democracy is still in fairly good health and our stability strong enough for now, or or it could quickly drag us further down the spiral of regression. Opposition parties have called time on the ANC’s dominance. The political temperature has not been this high since 1994. Twenty election candidates have been murdered and hundreds of millions of rands lost through damage to property during political protests. Politicians – and President Jacob Zuma – used pre-election rhetoric of a kind not seen before. The main reason probably was because the past week’s election was the prelude to the mother of all elections in 2019 – and more was at stake than merely the number of wards or councils lost or won. During one of the last ANC rallies, President Jacob Zuma told thousands of supporters in Zulu: “The oppressors still control the economy. The black nation must unite until the land is returned.” The appeal was blatant and painted the DA – the biggest opposition party – as a “white” organisation that must be fought by South Africa’s black majority. At campaign rally after campaign rally, the President has recalled the battles of the apartheid era, denounding the DA as a “poisonous snake” filled with “hatred” of black people. High and rising unemployment, corruption and poor service delivery have been some of the main issues dominating the election campaign. At least 26% of South Africans are without work. The ANC has been hit by a string of scandals this year – the Concourt ruling that President Zuma should personally be held liable to pay back millions of his Nkandla home, the High Court ruling that charges should be reinstated against him in regard with the Spy Tapes saga and the alleged involvement of the Gupta family in what was coined “State Capture”. According to Municipal IQ, a data and intelligence service specilaising in the monitoring and assessment of South Africa’s 287 municipalities, there were at least 70 violent protests over a lack of decent housing, other service delivery issues and education since the beginning of the year. In 2015, there were 44 protests within the same period. The unresponsiveness of government is a driver of community protest, but it is not the only driver of dissent. Commentators say one cannot separate local government from thje socio-economic conditions in which it operates. The ANC knew that if current trends continued and it got less that 60% of the electoral support, there would be a realistic chance that it could get less than 50% of the vote in 2019. And there is the chance that if the EFF didn’t at least doubled its support of 6% in the 2014 general election, South Africans would not take it as seriously as they did until now. But what will the results reflect? And with a voting day that more or less ran smoothly and without the violence that was expected, do South Africans feel more positive about the years ahead and what the general election of 2019 will bring us? How many of the 26,3 million registered voters drew their crosses? At the 2011 local government election, 23 million people were registered, but only 11 million voted. South Africans will probably feel even more positive if the coalitions between political parties to govern cities and towns actually work and last. But can political parties like the ANC and the DA or the ANC and the EFF govern together and will they even consider coalition to create a better future for the citizens of our country? And if the ANC doesn’t get an outright majority in 2019, the whole country will have to be governed by a coalition. That could mean a serious test for stability and effective government. How do political parties that govern municipalities and councils obtain stability and progress? What is necessary to get that universal political reality of a strong centre and a solid middle ground? What will this election’s results show? There were three highly contested Metro’s – Johannesburg, Tswane and Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality in Port Elizabeth. Rustenburg in Northwest might for the first time fall into the governing hands of the EFF. In 2011, the ANC managed to secure control of 198 councils, winning in seven of the country’s eight biggest Metropolitian areas. Some 40% of the country live in those areas. In contrast, the DA, with Cape Town under its control, managed 18 councils. Beaufort-West was the only municipality in the Western Cape that was still managed by the ANC. How much support will 35-year old leftist firebrand, Julius Malema, leader of the EFF, get? And will the EFF form coalitions with the DA in order to oust the ANC in some municipalities? South Africa is one of the most powerful engines in the African economy, yet many will argue that the ANC’s policies have led to the economic stagnation and rising unemployment. If the leading party’s results are worse than expected, and internal revolt could force President Zuma to quit, leading to economic reforms that could boost growth in South Africa and the rest of the continent. But a strong ANC majority would keep him in power and allow him to influence the succession until he steps down in 2019. The country is hurting economically. Since the currency plunged to record lows in December after President Zuma fired former Finance Minister Nhlanha Nene, the International Monetary Fund has slashed its forecast for South Africa, projecting growth of only 0,1 percent this year. And the central bank is now forecasting zero growth this year.
